Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

In Florida, a home insured by Citizens Property Insurance with wind coverage must also carry flood insurance. In a high-risk zone (A or V) this has applied since 2023 (new policies from April 1, renewals from July 1), whatever the home is worth. Outside those zones it phases in by rebuilding cost: from January 1, 2026 at $400,000 or more, and from January 1, 2027 for all other Citizens homes. Condo-unit and no-wind policies are exempt.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

77.9% of Broward County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 77.9% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood.

Flooded? Work out the proof-of-loss deadline for an NFIP (National Flood Insurance Program) policy. If the President declares a major disaster or emergency for your area, FEMA's standard window to register for disaster aid is 60 days from that declaration date, and FEMA can extend it (44 CFR §206.112). A private (non-NFIP) flood policy sets its own claim deadlines; they are in that policy.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 35,049 NFIP flood claims and $456.6 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2023, 2024 and 2017.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2023 ($249,212,146), 2024 ($35,107,673), 2017 ($24,329,084). Total paid $456,568,107. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 35,049 claims since 1978 against 234,789 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 32.6% of the 43,646 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 43,646 policies reporting one)32.6%Florida: 38.6%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)86.3%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 16,418 claims paid with a damage figure)0.5%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk with waves; B and shaded X are moderate risk; C and unshaded X are minimal risk; D is not yet studied.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? Since FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0, price is set from each building's own flood risk, not its zone, and these are existing policies whose buildings differ. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

46.4% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $643, full-risk $673 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$643
  • Median full-risk premium$673
  • Pay below full-risk46.4% of 98,708Florida: 49.8%

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

The usual building deductible here is $1,250 (50.0% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways to lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

How much flood risk is here?

Very High for coastal flooding and Very High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $14.1 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: coastal flood loss here is higher than in about 71% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $289.0 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 66% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $166.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $535 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.
